pos: adj. (saying one thing to one man and another to the next; disqualifying in a deacon)
etymology: From double + tongued. Paul's Greek is dilogos, literally two-worded — a man whose account of a matter changes with his audience. It appears once in Scripture, in a list of things a deacon must not be.
biblical_def: The qualifications for a deacon begin with four negatives, and the first is about speech: “Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre” (1 Timothy 3:8). The office is practical — the men who handled the daily distribution in Acts 6 — and it requires a man who carries the same account into every room, because a servant of the church moves between parties and hears both. What such a man must hold is stated next: “Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience” (1 Timothy 3:9), and the church is told to test before it appoints: “And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless” (1 Timothy 3:10). James treats the same fault as a monstrosity in any Christian: “Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be” (James 3:10). And Paul gives the positive rule for all love: “Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good” (Romans 12:9). A double tongue is not a lie exactly; it is two truths arranged so that neither party can check them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines doubletongued as making contrary declarations on the same subject at different times; deceitful.
webster_full: DOUBLE-TONGUED, a. Making contrary declarations on the same subject at different times; deceitful.
DOUBLE, a. Deceitful; acting two parts, one openly, the other in secret.
DEACON, n. [Gr. a servant or minister.] A person in the lowest degree of holy orders; in Scripture, an officer of the church chosen to attend to its temporal concerns.
GRAVE, a. Of weighty character; not light or trifling; serious; sober; solemn.
DISSIMULATION, n. The act of dissembling; a hiding under a false appearance; a feigning; false pretension; hypocrisy.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 3:8
Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre;
1 Timothy 3:9
Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.
1 Timothy 3:10
And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.
James 3:10
Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.
corruption_summary: Saying different things to different audiences is renamed diplomacy or pastoral sensitivity, and a disqualifying fault becomes a professional skill.
corruption_paragraphs: The double tongue is rarely defended; it is simply renamed. A leader tells the concerned party one version and the accused party another, and calls it wisdom in handling a delicate situation. Paul treats it as a bar to office, set beside drunkenness and greed. The reason is structural: a deacon hears the complaints of a congregation and moves between the offended and the offending, and a man who adjusts his account to his hearer makes reconciliation impossible — each party is now working from different facts and will never discover why they cannot agree.

The distinction that must be kept is between a double tongue and ordinary discretion. Scripture nowhere requires a man to say everything he knows to everyone; it forbids saying contrary things. Proverbs commends the man who covereth a transgression and the faithful spirit that concealeth a matter. Silence is not duplicity. What 1 Timothy 3:8 forbids is the second account — the version manufactured for a particular room, which exists to purchase that room's goodwill at the expense of the truth another room was given.
roots_summary: Greek dilogos (G1351), double-worded; diakonos (G1249), a servant, deacon; semnos (G4586), grave, dignified; anupokritos (G505), without hypocrisy.
roots_lines: Greek dilogos (G1351) — two-worded, doubletongued; only 1 Timothy 3:8.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant, deacon; the office of Acts 6 and 1 Timothy 3.
Greek semnos (G4586) — grave, worthy of respect; the first requirement in the list.
Greek anupokritos (G505) — unfeigned, without hypocrisy; Romans 12:9, love without dissimulation.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, prove; 1 Timothy 3:10, let these first be proved.
usage: “Not doubletongued” — beside drunkenness and greed, as a bar to office.
“Let these also first be proved” — the church tests before it appoints.
“These things ought not so to be” — James, on one mouth and two messages.

pos: adj. (fainthearted; small-souled under pressure — not defective in intellect)
etymology: From feeble + minded. Paul's Greek is oligopsuchos, small-souled — the discouraged and fainthearted. The English word has since narrowed to mean intellectual disability, which the Greek does not mean at all.
biblical_def: Paul gives a congregation four different duties toward four different kinds of member, and the differences matter: “Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men” (1 Thessalonians 5:14). The unruly get a warning; the fainthearted get comfort; the weak get a prop under them; and everyone gets patience. Treating the fainthearted man as though he were unruly — scolding a discouraged soul — is a failure of pastoral care, and so is comforting a man who needs to be warned. Paul repeats the burden on those who can bear it: “We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves” (Romans 15:1). The pattern is Christ's own, prophesied by Isaiah: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth” (Isaiah 42:3), and Matthew records the fulfilment in the middle of a Sabbath controversy: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory” (Matthew 12:20). A reed already bruised and a wick already smoking are the two things easiest to finish off, and He does not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines feeble-minded as weak in mind; wanting firmness or constancy; irresolute — the older sense of faintheartedness rather than intellectual defect.
webster_full: FEEBLE-MINDED, a. Weak in mind; wanting firmness or constancy; irresolute.
FEEBLE, a. [Fr. faible.] Weak; destitute of much physical strength; wanting force or vigor.
FAINT-HEARTED, a. Cowardly; timorous; dejected; easily depressed, or yielding to fear.
COMFORT, v.t. To strengthen the mind under affliction; to console; to give new vigor to the spirits.
SUPPORT, v.t. [L. supporto.] To bear; to sustain; to uphold; to keep from falling.
scriptures: 1 Thessalonians 5:14
Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men.
Romans 15:1
We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
Isaiah 42:3
A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth.
Matthew 12:20
A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory.
corruption_summary: An English word that has shifted since 1611 makes a tender apostolic command sound like a slur, and the distinct pastoral duty it names is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The problem is a genuine shift in English. Feebleminded now means intellectually disabled, and a modern reader hears Paul categorizing people cruelly. His oligopsuchos means small-souled — the discouraged, the fainthearted, the believer whose courage has run out. The principle to recover is that 1 Thessalonians 5:14 names four distinct pastoral duties, and the value of the verse lies entirely in not confusing them.

The practical failure is common and costly. A congregation with one register — all exhortation, or all comfort — will damage half its members. The unruly man treated tenderly is confirmed in his disorder; the fainthearted man warned is crushed by the very people who should have strengthened him. Isaiah 42:3 is the standard, and it is set in a prophecy about a King bringing forth judgment: He is not indulgent, and He does not break what is already bent. A church that can only rebuke has not learned the first thing about the Servant it preaches.
roots_summary: Greek oligopsuchos (G3642), small-souled, fainthearted; paramutheomai (G3888), to comfort, encourage; antechomai (G472), to hold firmly to, support; ataktos (G813), disorderly.
roots_lines: Greek oligopsuchos (G3642) — small of soul, fainthearted; only 1 Thessalonians 5:14.
Greek ataktos (G813) — out of rank, unruly; the ones to be warned, not comforted.
Greek paramutheomai (G3888) — to speak near, encourage; the duty owed the fainthearted.
Greek antechomai (G472) — to cling to, hold up; the prop under the weak.
Hebrew qaneh ratsuts (H7070 + H7533) — a bruised reed; Isaiah 42:3.
usage: “Warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded” — and never the reverse.
“Bear the infirmities of the weak” — the burden falls on the strong.
“A bruised reed shall he not break” — the standard, and He is the King.

pos: n. pl. (men who conceal what they are; the company David refused)
etymology: From Latin dissimulare, to make unlike, to disguise. Psalm 26:4 renders Hebrew naalamim, the hidden ones — men whose real character is concealed. The word names an act of hiding, not merely of lying.
biblical_def: David describes the company he will not keep: “I have not sat with vain persons, neither will I go in with dissemblers” (Psalm 26:4). The Hebrew calls them the hidden ones — men whose visible life and actual life are different things — and the psalmist's point is about association rather than judgment: he will not sit with them. The next verse is stronger still: “I have hated the congregation of evil doers; and will not sit with the wicked” (Psalm 26:5), where the word congregation hints that the assembly itself can be the problem. Paul gives the New Testament form of the same resolve, and joins it to love rather than setting it against love: “Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good” (Romans 12:9). Love unfeigned is love that has stopped performing. And Galatians names the self-deception under the concealment: “For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself” (Galatians 6:3). The dissembler practises on others first and becomes his own best audience, which is the state Scripture treats as the hardest to leave.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dissembler as one who dissembles; a hypocrite; one who conceals his opinions or dispositions under a false appearance.
webster_full: DISSEMBLER, n. One who dissembles; a hypocrite; one who conceals his opinions or dispositions under a false appearance.
DISSEMBLE, v.t. [L. dissimulo; dis and similis, like.] To hide under a false appearance; to conceal; to disguise; to pretend that not to be which really is.
DISSIMULATION, n. The act of dissembling; a hiding under a false appearance; a feigning; false pretension; hypocrisy.
HYPOCRITE, n. [Gr. a stage-player.] One who feigns to be what he is not; one who has the form of godliness without the power.
FEIGN, v.t. [L. fingo.] To invent or imagine; to make a show of; to pretend; to assume a false appearance.
scriptures: Psalm 26:4
I have not sat with vain persons, neither will I go in with dissemblers.
Psalm 26:5
I have hated the congregation of evil doers; and will not sit with the wicked.
Romans 12:9
Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.
Galatians 6:3
For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself.
corruption_summary: Sincerity is redefined as authenticity — being visibly whatever one presently feels — which produces a new species of performance rather than an end to performing.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern antidote to dissembling is authenticity, and it has produced a second kind of theatre. A person curates a visible struggle, narrates a doubt, displays a wound, and is applauded for honesty; the audience has changed and the performance has not. Romans 12:9 sets the standard higher than transparency: let love be without dissimulation, which asks whether the love is real, not whether the feelings are broadcast. A man can be completely open about himself and still not love anyone.

Psalm 26 is uncomfortable in the other direction and should not be softened. David refuses to sit with dissemblers, and verse 5 says he hates the congregation of evil doers. Scripture does not treat every association as neutral; bad company corrupts good manners, and a man is shaped by the table he sits at. This is not a licence for a sect — Christ was called the friend of publicans and sinners, and David goes on in the psalm to ask God to examine and prove him. The distinction is between eating with sinners in order to call them and belonging to a company whose habit is concealment.
roots_summary: Hebrew naalam (H5956), to hide oneself, be concealed; shav (H7723), vanity, emptiness; Greek anupokritos (G505), unfeigned; hupokrites (G5273), a play-actor.
roots_lines: Hebrew naalam (H5956) — to be hidden, concealed; Psalm 26:4, the hidden ones.
Hebrew methe shav (H7723) — men of vanity; the vain persons of the same verse.
Greek anupokritos (G505) — without play-acting; Romans 12:9, love without dissimulation.
Greek hupokrites (G5273) — a stage-player behind a mask; Christ's word for the Pharisees.
Greek phrenapatao (G5422) — to deceive one's own mind; Galatians 6:3.
usage: “Neither will I go in with dissemblers” — a question of company, not of verdict.
“Let love be without dissimulation” — is the love real, not is the feeling published.
“He deceiveth himself” — the dissembler's last audience.

pos: n. pl. (rivalries; jealous competition, listed among the works of the flesh)
etymology: From Latin aemulatio, rivalry. Paul's Greek is zeloi, the plural of zelos — the same root as zeal, which can be holy or poisonous. In the plural it is the competitive jealousy that sets Christians against each other.
biblical_def: Paul's catalogue of the works of the flesh is not a list of pagan vices; the majority are sins a church commits against itself: “Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies” (Galatians 5:20). Emulations stand between variance and wrath, in a run of eight words about people who cannot get along. The warning that follows is severe: “Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5:21). He then names the engine driving the rivalry: “Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another” (Galatians 5:26) — empty glory, sought at another's expense. And James traces the consequences: “For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work” (James 3:16). The word is worth its place because the root is neutral. The same zelos is used of the zeal of God's house that ate the Lord Jesus up. Zeal aimed at God's glory is a virtue; aimed at one's own standing among brethren, it is in a list with witchcraft.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines emulation as the desire of superiority, attended with an endeavor to surpass others; and, in a bad sense, an ambitious rivalry, accompanied with envy or a desire to depress another.
webster_full: EMULATION, n. [L. aemulatio.] The desire of superiority, attended with an endeavor to surpass others; rivalry.
EMULATION, n. An ardor kindled by the praiseworthy examples of others, inciting to imitate them, or to equal or exceed them.
EMULATION, n. In a bad sense, an ambitious rivalry accompanied with envy, or a desire to depress another.
ENVY, n. [L. invidia.] Pain, uneasiness, mortification or discontent, excited by the sight of another's superiority or success.
VAINGLORY, n. Glory that is vain, empty or false; pride above desert, or above the merit of the person.
scriptures: Galatians 5:20
Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies,
Galatians 5:21
Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.
Galatians 5:26
Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another.
James 3:16
For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.
corruption_summary: Rivalry between Christians is dignified as a healthy zeal for truth, so that a work of the flesh is practised in the vocabulary of faithfulness.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 5:20 is a list a doctrinally serious congregation should read slowly, because eight of the seventeen works of the flesh are things done inside a church by people with convictions. Hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, envyings. Every one of them can be conducted in the language of contending for the faith, and each has been. Paul does not exempt the man who is right about the doctrine. A true position advanced to defeat a brother and raise oneself is a work of the flesh, and it appears in the same sentence as witchcraft.

Verse 26 supplies the test, and it is diagnostic rather than doctrinal: desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another. Whose reputation is being built? Who is being provoked, and does the provoking feel enjoyable? Is another man's standing a grief? The remedy in the chapter is not less conviction but a different source of life — walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. Paul's answer to fleshly rivalry is never a milder zeal; it is a zeal with a different object.
roots_summary: Greek zelos (G2205), zeal, jealousy, rivalry; phthonos (G5355), envy; kenodoxia (G2754), vainglory; eritheia (G2052), factious self-seeking.
roots_lines: Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal or jealousy; holy in John 2:17, fleshly in the plural at Galatians 5:20.
Greek phthonos (G5355) — envy; the next item in Paul's list, verse 21.
Greek kenodoxos (G2755) — desirous of empty glory; Galatians 5:26, the engine of the rivalry.
Greek eritheia (G2052) — self-seeking faction; James 3:16, with envying.
Greek akatastasia (G181) — confusion, disorder; what envying and strife produce.
usage: “Hatred, variance, emulations” — eight of the seventeen are church sins.
“Desirous of vain glory” — whose reputation is being built.
“There is confusion and every evil work” — the reliable fruit.

pos: adj. (leading to destruction; of the heresies false teachers bring in privily)
etymology: From Latin damnare, to condemn. Peter's Greek is haireseis apoleias, heresies of destruction — a Hebraic genitive naming not merely their character but their end. The word describes where a teaching arrives, not how it sounds.
biblical_def: Peter warns that the pattern of the old covenant will repeat in the new: “But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction” (2 Peter 2:1). Three things are named. The method is privily — smuggled in alongside, never announced. The content is a denial of the Lord. The end is destruction, which is what damnable means. The consequence falls on outsiders too: “And many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of” (2 Peter 2:2). The motive is money: “And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you: whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their damnation slumbereth not” (2 Peter 2:3) — a congregation regarded as inventory. Paul had said the same to the Ephesian elders with a different figure: “For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock” (Acts 20:29). Both apostles expect it, and both expect it from inside.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines damnable as that may be damned or condemned; deserving damnation; worthy of condemnation or censure; pernicious.
webster_full: DAMNABLE, a. That may be damned or condemned; deserving damnation; worthy of eternal punishment.
DAMNABLE, a. In a low or ludicrous sense, odious; detestable; pernicious.
DAMNATION, n. Sentence or condemnation to everlasting punishment; the state of eternal torments.
HERESY, n. [Gr. to take, a choosing.] A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
PERNICIOUS, a. [L. perniciosus.] Destructive; having the quality of killing, destroying or injuring.
scriptures: 2 Peter 2:1

But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.
2 Peter 2:2
And many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of.
2 Peter 2:3
And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you: whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their damnation slumbereth not.
Acts 20:29
For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.
corruption_summary: Heresy is treated as a word belonging to an intolerant past, so a category the apostles use to protect a flock is retired just where it is needed.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern objection is that naming heresy is unloving, and it collapses on Peter's own reasoning. He is not defending an institution's boundary; he is warning sheep about wolves, and the mark of the wolf is that it comes in privily, not announcing itself. A shepherd who will not name the danger has chosen his own reputation for graciousness over the safety of the flock. Verse 3 shows what is actually at stake for the people involved: they are made merchandise of, treated as a revenue base by men with feigned words.

The opposite abuse is real and must be named too, because the word heretic has been thrown at faithful men by every establishment the Reformation confronted. The discipline is to keep the category narrow and biblical. Peter defines it precisely — denying the Lord that bought them — and Paul's lists run to the resurrection, the gospel, the Person of Christ. A church that calls every disagreement heresy has spent the word, and will have nothing left to say when a man arrives who really does deny the Lord.
roots_summary: Greek apoleia (G684), destruction, perdition; hairesis (G139), a chosen party, heresy; pareisago (G3919), to bring in alongside; emporeuomai (G1710), to make merchandise of.
roots_lines: Greek apoleia (G684) — destruction; heresies of destruction, rendered damnable.
Greek hairesis (G139) — a self-chosen party or opinion; the root of heresy and of faction.
Greek pareisago (G3919) — to bring in alongside, smuggle in; the method, privily.
Greek emporeuomai (G1710) — to trade in, make merchandise of; the flock as inventory.
Greek lukos barus (G3074) — a grievous wolf; Acts 20:29, Paul's figure for the same men.
usage: “Privily shall bring in damnable heresies” — smuggled, never announced.
“Make merchandise of you” — a congregation as a revenue base.
“Grievous wolves…not sparing the flock” — and they come from inside.

pos: n. (a collection gathered for the relief of poor saints)
etymology: From Latin contribuere, to bring together. Paul's Greek here is koinonia — fellowship — which is the striking thing about the verse: the money is called by the same word used for the communion of saints.
biblical_def: Paul reports a collection taken by Greek churches for Jewish believers they had never met: “For it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem” (Romans 15:26). The Greek word behind contribution is koinonia, fellowship — Paul does not regard the money as the material support of a spiritual fellowship but as the fellowship itself in one of its forms. The Macedonians, who were poor, had to ask for the privilege: “Praying us with much intreaty that we would receive the gift, and take upon us the fellowship of the ministering to the saints” (2 Corinthians 8:4). What the giving produced was not gratitude toward the givers but worship: “Whiles by the experiment of this ministration they glorify God for your professed subjection unto the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men” (2 Corinthians 9:13). And Paul's method was unglamorous and weekly: “Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come” (1 Corinthians 16:2) — every one, proportionate, laid by in advance, so that no emotional appeal would be needed when he arrived.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contribution as the act of giving to a common stock, or in common with others; the payment of each person's share of some common expense; that which is given to a common stock or purpose.
webster_full: CONTRIBUTION, n. The act of giving to a common stock, or in common with others; the act of lending a portion of power or influence to a common purpose.
CONTRIBUTION, n. That which is given to a common stock or purpose, either by an individual or by many.
CONTRIBUTE, v.t. [L. contribuo; con and tribuo, to give.] To give or grant in common with others; to give to a common stock or for a common purpose.
COLLECTION, n. A gathering of money for charitable or other purposes; the sum collected.
ALMS, n. [Gr. mercy.] Any thing given gratuitously to relieve the poor, as money, food, or clothing.
scriptures: Romans 15:26
For it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem.
2 Corinthians 8:4
Praying us with much intreaty that we would receive the gift, and take upon us the fellowship of the ministering to the saints.
2 Corinthians 9:13
Whiles by the experiment of this ministration they glorify God for your professed subjection unto the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men;
1 Corinthians 16:2
Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come.
corruption_summary: Church giving becomes either a fundraising operation driven by appeal and pressure, or a private matter with no bearing on the fellowship it is called a part of.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 16:2 describes a method built to make appeals unnecessary. Weekly, by every member, proportioned to how God has prospered him, laid by in advance — that there be no gatherings when I come. Paul is deliberately removing the moment of pressure. Compare the modern appeal, engineered for the peak of feeling, with the sum determined by the strength of the presentation. The apostolic arrangement is closer to an ordinary discipline than to an event, and it asks nothing of a man that his own ledger cannot supply.

The other error privatizes it entirely. Paul calls the money koinonia, the word for the fellowship of the saints, and the Macedonians begged for the privilege of it while being, he says, in deep poverty. Giving is not the maintenance budget of a fellowship; it is one of the things fellowship is. And 2 Corinthians 9:13 names the end: the recipients glorify God. Not the donor, and not the church that organized it. A collection that produces thanksgiving toward men has been arranged wrongly somewhere.
roots_summary: Greek koinonia (G2842), fellowship, sharing, contribution; diakonia (G1248), ministry, service; leitourgia (G3009), a public service; euodoo (G2137), to prosper.
roots_lines: Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship; rendered contribution at Romans 15:26.
Greek diakonia (G1248) — ministry, service; the ministering to the saints, 2 Corinthians 8:4.
Greek hapoles / haplotes (G572) — singleness, liberality; the liberal distribution of 9:13.
Greek euodoo (G2137) — to be prospered; 1 Corinthians 16:2, the measure of each man's portion.
Greek logeia (G3048) — a collection; the gathering Paul did not want to make on arrival.
usage: “A certain contribution for the poor saints” — and the word is fellowship.
“Praying us with much intreaty” — the poor asked for the privilege.
“That there be no gatherings when I come” — a method built against pressure.

pos: n. (the whole apparatus of deceiving; the working of the man of sin)
etymology: From deceivable + -ness. Paul's Greek is apate adikias, the deceit of unrighteousness. The KJV's heavy compound catches the sense of a deceiving that is systematic and equipped — not a single lie but a whole capacity for it.
biblical_def: Paul describes the last great deception and is careful about who is finally deceived: “And with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved” (2 Thessalonians 2:10). The last clause is the ground of the whole thing. They perish not because the deception was too clever but because they did not love the truth — and a man who does not love the truth is defenceless against a lie he finds agreeable. The equipment is genuinely impressive: “Even him, whose coming is after the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders” (2 Thessalonians 2:9). Signs and wonders are not by themselves evidence of God, which Deuteronomy 13 had already established. And the judicial consequence is terrible: “And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie” (2 Thessalonians 2:11) — God giving men over to what they preferred. Paul traces the same appetite in ordinary church life: “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears” (2 Timothy 4:3). The hearers do the heaping. Deception is a market, and it has buyers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deceivableness as liableness to be deceived, and the quality of being deceptive or apt to mislead.
webster_full: DECEIVABLENESS, n. Liableness to be deceived. Also, the quality of being deceptive or apt to deceive.
DECEIVABLE, a. Subject to deceit or imposture; exposed to imposition. Also, deceitful; apt to mislead.
DECEIVE, v.t. [L. decipio; de and capio, to take.] To mislead the mind; to cause to err; to cause to believe what is false, or disbelieve what is true.
DELUSION, n. [L. deludo.] The act of deluding; deception; a misleading of the mind; false representation.
IMPOSTURE, n. Deception practiced under a false or assumed character, with a view to impose on others.
scriptures: 2 Thessalonians 2:10
And with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved.
2 Thessalonians 2:9
Even him, whose coming is after the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders,
2 Thessalonians 2:11
And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie:
2 Timothy 4:3
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
corruption_summary: Deception is treated as a failure of information, so that the remedy sought is more evidence, when Paul locates the failure in a heart that did not love the truth.
corruption_paragraphs: The assumption behind most modern apologetics is that people believe wrong things because they have not seen the right facts. 2 Thessalonians 2:10 gives a different diagnosis: because they received not the love of the truth. Not the truth — the love of it. A man may know a thing and not want it, and such a man will be taken by any deception that flatters what he does want. This is why verse 9 can grant the deceiver real power and real wonders without conceding anything. Signs prove nothing about a message; Deuteronomy 13 says that even a sign that comes to pass does not authorize a prophet who leads after other gods.

Verse 11 is the hardest clause in the passage and it is not an exception to God's justice but an expression of it. God shall send them strong delusion. Romans 1 has the same judicial pattern three times over — God gave them up, gave them up, gave them over. The sentence on a man who will not have the truth is to be handed what he preferred. And 2 Timothy 4:3 shows the mechanism running at congregational scale: the people heap up teachers to themselves, which means the false teacher is usually a supply raised by a demand.
roots_summary: Greek apate (G539), deceit, delusion; adikia (G93), unrighteousness; plane (G4106), a wandering, delusion; knetho (G2833), to itch.
roots_lines: Greek apate (G539) — deceit; apate adikias, the deceit of unrighteousness, 2 Thessalonians 2:10.
Greek energeia planes (G1753 + G4106) — a working of delusion; verse 11, strong delusion.
Greek teras pseudous (G5059) — a lying wonder; verse 9, real power and a false witness.
Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be healthy, sound; sound doctrine, 2 Timothy 4:3.
Greek knetho (G2833) — to tickle, itch; the ears that do the heaping.
usage: “They received not the love of the truth” — the diagnosis is of the heart.
“Signs and lying wonders” — real power, and no credential.
“Heap to themselves teachers” — the hearers do the heaping.

pos: n. (the smallest unclean creature; half of Christ's proverb against the Pharisees)
etymology: From Old English gnaett. The Greek konops is the smallest of the unclean creatures, the camel the largest; the proverb depends on both being unclean by the law, so that the straining and the swallowing are the same kind of act at opposite scales.
biblical_def: Christ's charge against the scribes is not that they were too strict but that their strictness was selective: “Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel” (Matthew 23:24). The picture is of a man filtering his drink through a cloth to catch an insect too small to matter and then, in the same swallow, taking down the largest unclean animal in Palestine. The verse before gives the actual instance: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone” (Matthew 23:23). The last clause is the one most often dropped, and it settles the meaning. Christ does not tell them to stop tithing their herbs. He tells them they should have done the small thing and not left the great things undone. Precision is not the fault; the fault is a precision that never reaches judgment, mercy, and faith. Paul warns of a related failure in the assembly: “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears” (2 Timothy 4:3) — and James names what any such straining reliably yields: “For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work” (James 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the gnat as a small insect, or rather a genus of insects, the Culex — and notes the Scripture proverb of straining at a gnat.
webster_full: GNAT, n. [Sax. gnaet.] A small insect, or rather a genus of insects, the Culex, with a proboscis armed with a sting.
GNAT, n. Any thing proverbially small; as, to strain at a gnat and swallow a camel.
STRAIN, v.t. To filter; to purify or separate from extraneous matter by filtration.
TITHE, n. [Sax. teotha, tenth.] The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock.
SCRUPULOUS, a. Nicely doubtful; hesitating to determine or to act, for fear of offending or doing wrong; cautious in decision.
scriptures: Matthew 23:24
Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel.
Matthew 23:23

Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
2 Timothy 4:3
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
James 3:16
For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.
corruption_summary: The proverb is used to dismiss care about small obediences altogether, when Christ's own sentence commands the small thing and the great thing together.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 23:24 has become the standing proof-text for anyone who finds a scruple inconvenient. Somebody objects to a practice, and is told not to strain at gnats. Verse 23 makes that use impossible: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. Christ affirms the herb tithe. What He condemns is a religion whose whole energy goes into the measurable small thing while judgment, mercy, and faith are left unattended. The proverb is not against precision; it is against a precision that has become a substitute.

The reason the figure works is that both creatures are unclean. The Pharisee straining his cup was obeying a real principle of the law and doing it carefully, and then swallowing a camel — the same uncleanness at maximum scale — without noticing. That is the permanent shape of the sin, and it is native to careful people. A church can conduct a two-year controversy over a matter of order while a member's family is destroyed by an unaddressed cruelty. Christ lists the three great matters by name so that no one has to guess which ones are the camels.
roots_summary: Greek konops (G2971), a gnat; kamelos (G2574), a camel; diulizo (G1368), to strain out; barus (G926), weighty.
roots_lines: Greek konops (G2971) — a gnat; only Matthew 23:24, the smallest unclean creature.
Greek kamelos (G2574) — a camel; unclean by Leviticus 11:4, and the largest beast at hand.
Greek diulizo (G1368) — to strain through; the filtering cloth over the cup.
Greek barutera tou nomou (G926) — the weightier matters of the law; judgment, mercy, faith.
Greek aphiemi (G863) — to leave, omit; what they did with the weightier matters.
usage: “Strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel” — both unclean, at opposite scales.
“These ought ye to have done” — the herb tithe is affirmed.
“Judgment, mercy, and faith” — the camels, named so no one need guess.

pos: adv. (freely, without charge or condition; of a creditor forgiving two debtors)
etymology: From Old French franc, free — the Franks being the free people of their territory. Luke's Greek is charizomai, from charis, grace: to forgive as a free gift. Frankly in 1611 means freely, not candidly.
biblical_def: Christ, dining with a Pharisee who is scandalized by the woman washing His feet, answers with a parable about arithmetic: “There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty” (Luke 7:41). Then the point on which everything turns: “And when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both. Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most?” (Luke 7:42). Frankly is freely — the debt was not reduced, rescheduled, or partly worked off. Both debtors had nothing, and both were released outright. Simon answers correctly that the one forgiven most will love most, and Christ applies it: “Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little” (Luke 7:47). The woman's love is the evidence of a forgiveness already received, not its purchase price — the parable Christ has just told makes the order unmistakable, since the creditor forgave before either debtor felt anything. And the danger in the room was never the woman's: “For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself” (Galatians 6:3). Simon owed fifty and thought he owed nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines frankly as without reserve, constraint or disguise; liberally; freely; readily — and cites the Scripture sense of freely giving.
webster_full: FRANKLY, adv. Openly; freely; ingenuously; without reserve, constraint or disguise.
FRANKLY, adv. Liberally; freely; readily; as, he frankly forgave them both.
FRANK, a. [Fr. franc, free.] Open; ingenuous; candid; free in uttering real sentiments; liberal; generous.
FORGIVE, v.t. To pardon; to remit, as an offense or debt; to overlook an offense, and treat the offender as not guilty.
CREDITOR, n. [L. creditor.] A person to whom a sum of money or other thing is due, by borrowing or purchase.
scriptures: Luke 7:41
There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty.
Luke 7:42
And when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both. Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most?
Luke 7:47
Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little.
Galatians 6:3
For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself.
corruption_summary: Verse 47 is read as though the woman's love purchased her forgiveness, reversing the order the parable in verses 41 and 42 was told to establish.
corruption_paragraphs: Her sins…are forgiven; for she loved much looks, in isolation, like love earning pardon, and it has been read that way in defence of a merit-based scheme. The parable Christ has just told forbids it. The creditor forgave both debtors when they had nothing to pay, before any love was shown, and the question He put to Simon was which of them will love him most — a future consequence of a past release. The for of verse 47 is evidential, not causal: her love proves the forgiveness, as the Greek construction and the whole shape of the story require. The last clause of the verse confirms it, since a man who loves little is described as one to whom little is forgiven.

The other half of the passage is aimed at the host, and it is the half that a respectable congregation should feel. Simon is the fifty-pence debtor, and his problem is that he thinks the figure is zero. He has given Christ no water, no kiss, no oil — ordinary courtesies — while a woman off the street has not ceased to kiss His feet. Little forgiven, little loved. The coldness of a settled and well-behaved Christian is very often exactly this: not a want of feeling but a want of any estimate of the debt.
roots_summary: Greek charizomai (G5483), to give freely, forgive; charis (G5485), grace; daneistes (G1157), a creditor; chreopheiletes (G5533), a debtor.
roots_lines: Greek charizomai (G5483) — to forgive as a free gift; Luke 7:42, rendered frankly forgave.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace; the root of the verb, and the whole of the parable.
Greek daneistes (G1157) — a moneylender, creditor; only Luke 7:41.
Greek chreopheiletes (G5533) — a debtor; both men, at different sums.
Greek hoti (G3754) — for, because; evidential in verse 47, as the parable requires.
usage: “When they had nothing to pay” — the condition of both debtors.
“He frankly forgave them both” — freely, and before any love appeared.
“To whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little” — and Simon is the fifty.

pos: v. (distracted, drawn about; of Martha in her own kitchen)
etymology: From Old French combrer, to hinder or obstruct. Luke's Greek is perispaomai, literally dragged around — pulled in several directions at once. The word describes the motion, not the quantity, of the work.
biblical_def: Luke reports a domestic scene with unusual precision: “But Martha was cumbered about much serving, and came to him, and said, Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me” (Luke 10:40). The Greek says she was being dragged about — not that she was working too hard, but that she was being pulled in several directions. Her complaint is addressed to the right Person and contains two things she should not have said: an accusation that He does not care, and an instruction about what He should do. He answers her by name, twice, which in Scripture is the address of tenderness: “And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things” (Luke 10:41). Then the verdict, which is not a rebuke of hospitality but a ranking: “But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42). Martha's serving was a real service and it was for Him. What had gone wrong was that the many things had displaced the one, and the one was sitting in her house. Paul's counsel to a church faces the same disorder from the other side: “Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good” (Romans 12:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cumber as to check, stop or retard, as by a load or weight; to make motion difficult; to obstruct; to perplex or embarrass; to distract or trouble.
webster_full: CUMBER, v.t. [Fr. combrer.] To check, stop or retard, as by a load or weight; to make motion difficult; to obstruct.
CUMBER, v.t. To perplex or embarrass; to distract or trouble.
CUMBER, v.t. To trouble; to be troublesome to; to cause trouble or obstruction in.
ENCUMBER, v.t. To load; to clog; to impede motion with a load, burden, or any thing inconvenient to the limbs.
DISTRACT, v.t. [L. distraho, to draw apart.] To draw or turn the mind different ways; to perplex; to harass with contrary purposes.
scriptures: Luke 10:40
But Martha was cumbered about much serving, and came to him, and said, Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me.
Luke 10:41
And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things:
Luke 10:42
But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.
Romans 12:9
Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.
corruption_summary: The account is used to disparage practical service, or to excuse idleness as contemplation, when Christ's answer ranks two goods rather than condemning one.
corruption_paragraphs: The sermon that makes Martha the villain misreads the text and slanders a woman Scripture honours. John records that Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus; it is Martha who makes one of the great confessions of the Gospel, that He is the Christ, the Son of God. Hospitality is commanded everywhere in Scripture, and she was exercising it toward the Lord Himself. Christ does not tell her to stop serving. He tells her she is being dragged about by many things while one thing is needful, and the one thing was in the next room.

The opposite abuse uses Mary to excuse a man who will not work. Luke 10 sits immediately after the good Samaritan, who is commended precisely for the interruption of his journey by hard, practical, expensive service — and Luke put the two together. The order Christ establishes is not contemplation instead of service but hearing before serving: the one thing needful supplies what the many things are for. A life of service with no sitting at His feet becomes exactly what Martha's had become — work for Him, conducted in accusation against Him.
roots_summary: Greek perispaomai (G4049), to be drawn around, distracted; merimnao (G3309), to be anxious, careful; turbazo (G5182), to be troubled; diakonia (G1248), service.
roots_lines: Greek perispaomai (G4049) — to be dragged about; only Luke 10:40, rendered cumbered.
Greek merimnao (G3309) — to be anxious; careful in verse 41, and forbidden in Matthew 6:25.
Greek turbazo (G5182) — to be stirred up, troubled; the second verb of verse 41.
Greek diakonia (G1248) — service, ministry; the good thing Martha was doing.
Greek agathe meris (G18 + G3310) — the good part; Mary's choice, which shall not be taken away.
usage: “Cumbered about much serving” — dragged about, not merely busy.
“Martha, Martha” — the doubled name of tenderness.
“One thing is needful” — a ranking, not a condemnation.
